title: Massaman Curry
subtitle: thai massaman beef curry
excerpt: Massaman curry is a slow-cooked Thai beef curry with Persian-influenced spices including cinnamon, cardamom, and star anise. The sauce is rich, mildly sweet, and deeply aromatic. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: One of the mildest Thai curries, with roots in the Muslim communities of southern Thailand. The spice profile reflects centuries of trade with Persia and India.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently, adding a splash of water if the sauce has thickened.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half for an easy future meal.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day once the spices have had time to develop.

glossaryTerms.definition: A mild Thai curry paste with Persian-influenced spices such as cinnamon, cardamom, and star anise. The name is thought to derive from the word Muslim.
A sour paste made from the pulp of tamarind pods. It adds a distinctive fruity acidity to curries and sauces.

Heat the oil in a dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches until seared on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the shallots and cook for 3 minutes until softened. Add the cinnamon, cardamom, and star anise. Stir for 1 minute.
Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the coconut milk and stock. Bring to a simmer.
Cover and cook over low heat for 60 minutes. Add the potato and peanuts. Cook uncovered for a further 30 minutes until the beef is tender and the potato is cooked through.
Stir in the fish sauce, sugar, and tamarind paste. Taste and adjust the balance of sour, salty, and sweet.
Serve with steamed rice and lime wedges on the side.

attrs.problem: The beef is still tough at 90 minutes.
attrs.solution: Shin needs time. Keep the lid on and cook for another 20 to 30 minutes. Low and slow is the only way with this cut.
Remove the lid for the last 20 minutes of cooking. The sauce will reduce and thicken around the meat and potatoes.
Add more tamarind paste and fish sauce in small amounts. The sour-salty balance is what lifts a massaman from dull to vivid.

content.text: Massaman curry has been eaten in southern Thailand for centuries. It reflects the trade routes that brought Persian and Indian spices to the region. It is a festival dish in many Muslim Thai communities. The curry is mild enough for people who find other Thai curries too hot.
